readerTitle: Marketing starts long before the ad
caseNote: 가상 사례 (공구점 테이프, 바퀴 제조사, 치과 예약 소프트웨어) + 실제 문헌 인용 (Drucker, AMA 정의)
insight: 마케팅은 다 만든 뒤에 알리는 일이 아니다. 고객이 무엇을 중요하게 여기는지 먼저 알아내고, 제품·가격·판매 경로·메시지를 거기에 맞추는 일이다.
misconception: 마케팅은 곧 광고와 홍보다. 매출이 안 나오면 광고비를 늘리면 된다.

sources.text: Drucker, P. F. (1973). Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices. Harper & Row.
American Marketing Association, Definitions of Marketing (approved 2017)
바퀴 제조사, 치과 예약 앱, 테이프 장면은 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: Drucker 인용문("The aim of marketing is to make selling superfluous... the product or service fits him and sells itself")은 1973년 저서 Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices에 나옵니다. 게시 전 원문 문구와 쪽수를 확인하세요. 카드에는 앞부분만 직접 인용하고 나머지는 풀어 썼습니다.
AMA 정의(creating, communicating, delivering, exchanging offerings that have value)는 2017년 승인본 기준입니다. 게시 전 AMA 사이트에서 현재 문구를 다시 확인하세요.
바퀴 제조사 사례에는 구체적 수치를 넣지 않았습니다. "3주", "2일" 배송 기간은 설명용 가상 수치입니다.

cards.title: Nobody sold you that roll of tape.
body: Last week you grabbed a roll of tape at the hardware store. You didn't see an ad for it. You just picked the one at eye level, with a label that said what it does, at a price that felt fair.
No salesperson. No campaign. Yet someone decided the shelf, the label, the size and the price. That was marketing, and you never noticed it.

image.label: Hand reaching for a roll of tape on a store shelf
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 공구점 진열대 눈높이 칸에서 손이 테이프 한 롤을 집는 장면. 테이프 라벨에 "Holds 20 kg" 같은 쉬운 문구와 가격표. 진열대 위치, 라벨, 가격표에 작은 점선 동그라미로 '누군가 정한 것'임을 표시. 실제 브랜드 로고 금지.

cards.title: Your wheels are great. Sales are flat.
body: Your family factory makes heavy-duty wheels for warehouse carts. Quality is excellent, but sales haven't grown in three years. You have budget for one marketing push this quarter.

options.text: Ads in trade magazines and search, so more buyers hear your name
options.feedback: Reach helps if buyers already want what you offer. If something else is holding them back, you pay to tell more people about the same problem.

options.text: A new logo and website, so you look as good as you are
options.feedback: A sharper look can build trust, but it assumes looks are the problem. You spend the budget without learning why buyers pick someone else.

options.text: Two weeks with warehouse managers, learning how they choose and replace wheels
options.feedback: You delay any visible campaign. In return, you find out what actually decides the sale, and every later move gets aimed at it.

cards.title: The problem wasn't the wheel.
body: The managers didn't care much about wheel brands. They cared about broken carts on the night shift, and replacements that took **three weeks** to arrive.

So the factory changed things that never appear in an ad. It kept the most common sizes in stock for two-day shipping. It renamed the range by load, "carries 300 kg", instead of part codes. It started selling through the maintenance suppliers managers already called.
Reorders started climbing. The ad budget barely moved.

cards.title: What marketing is
body: **Marketing** is the work of understanding what customers value, then shaping what you offer, how you price it, where they find it and what you say, so the right customers choose you.
Advertising is one piece, and usually the last one. The wheel factory did marketing by listening first, then changing stock, names and sales channels. Talking came after.

image.label: Iceberg: ads above water, most of marketing below
image.brief: 빙산 인포그래픽. 수면 위 작은 부분에 "Ads". 수면 아래 큰 부분에 "Understanding customers", "What you offer", "Price", "Where it's sold", "What you say". 차분한 파란색 톤.

cards.title: Make selling almost unnecessary.
body: In 1973, management writer Peter Drucker put it sharply: "The aim of marketing is to make selling superfluous." His point was that if you understand customers well enough, the product fits them and largely sells itself.

The American Marketing Association's definition says the same in plainer terms. It lists **creating** value first, then communicating, delivering and exchanging it. Communication is in there. It just isn't the start.

cards.title: Every business already does marketing.
body: A bakery that notices office workers order at 7:30 and opens at 7:00 is doing marketing. So is a plumber who quotes a fixed price because customers fear surprise bills.
The question is never whether you do marketing. It's whether you do it on purpose, by asking customers, or by accident, by guessing.

image.label: Bakery opening early for a line of office workers
image.brief: 아침 7시 시계가 걸린 작은 빵집 문이 열리고, 정장 차림 직장인 몇 명이 줄 서 있는 장면. 빵집 주인이 메모장을 들고 손님에게 질문하는 모습. 실제 상호·로고 금지.

cards.title: Understanding isn't enough on its own.
body: A perfectly fitted product that nobody hears about still fails. Listening tells you what to build and say. You still have to say it, and keep saying it.
There's a second trap. If "everything is marketing", it can become nobody's job. Someone still needs to own the question: why do customers choose us, and what would make more of the right ones do it?

cards.title: Now it's a software app.
body: You sell booking software to dental clinics. Many clinics start a free trial, but few pay. Your co-founder wants to hire an ad agency to double trial signups.

options.text: Hire the agency. More trials means more paying users
options.feedback: You get more trials quickly, but if most users leave for the same reason, you pay to fill a leaky bucket.

options.text: Watch a few trials and call clinics who left, then fix what you learn
options.feedback: Growth waits a few weeks. You learn whether setup, price or the pitch is the blocker, and later ad money lands on a product that converts.

options.text: Build the three features your loudest customer asked for
options.feedback: It is listening, which helps. But one vocal customer may not speak for the clinics that quietly walked away.

cards.title: Marketing is fitting your business to customers, then telling them.
body: Before spending more on getting noticed, check whether what you offer, how it's priced and where it's found match what customers actually value.
**Try it today:** ask three recent customers why they chose you over the alternative. Write their exact words down.
